rationale: The BSB hides this link. At 20:15 the landowner asks, "are you envious because I am generous?" (BSB); at 6:23 Jesus says, "if your eyes are bad, your whole body will be full of darkness" (BSB). In Greek both verses say ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός, "your eye [is] evil," in every edition Bible Hub lists (6:23 adds the subjunctive ᾖ). The Geneva Bible note on 20:15 draws the line itself: by an evil eye "the Hebrews mean envy," "as above in Mt 6:23," "the word being the same in that place as it is here," and the Expositor's Greek Testament on 20:15 refers the reader to its note on 6:22-24. The setting of 6:22-23 is money: it stands between "treasures in heaven" (6:20) and "You cannot serve both God and money" (6:24). A recurrence within one Gospel is motif (conn-matt18-forgive-matt6). The label is plausible rather than strong because the shared wording is certain but its sense at 6:23 is disputed: Thayer's entry for πονηρός, on Bible Hub, lists 6:23 under a physical sense ("diseased or blind") and notes that "others take πονηρός in Matthew and Luke as above ethically." If 6:23 speaks of a diseased eye, the two verses share an idiom and nothing more. Mark 7:22 has the same pair of words (ὀφθαλμὸς πονηρός), which the BSB renders "envy"; that verse is outside Matthew and is not part of this row.
